title: An early start is not a fixed script
objective: Explain how timing, dose and context qualify a prenatal risk claim.
hook: An early start is not a fixed script
story: A café poster claims that one early exposure determines a child’s future. Sam worries that a relative’s pregnancy history explains every later difficulty. Maya asks whether a risk factor can establish an individual cause.

concepts.title: Development starts before birth.

terms.Teratogen: an exposure that can disrupt prenatal development

points: Prenatal development: development before birth
Gestation: the course of pregnancy
Teratogen: an exposure that can disrupt prenatal development
concepts.text:
Gestation: the course of pregnancy. Teratogen: an exposure that can disrupt prenatal development.

Prenatal development involves changing biological systems. Some exposures can increase the risk of harm, and effects depend partly on when development is occurring.

This does not mean an exposure guarantees an outcome. Advice about a specific pregnancy belongs with a qualified healthcare professional who can evaluate the actual exposure.

concepts.title: Timing changes the question.
points: Sensitive period: time of heightened responsiveness
Dose: amount of exposure
Risk factor: condition associated with increased likelihood
concepts.text:
Sensitive period: time of heightened responsiveness. Risk factor: condition associated with increased likelihood.

A developing system can be more responsive to an exposure during particular periods. Dose, duration, nutrition, health and other exposures may also matter.

A population association does not show which factor caused a particular child’s difficulty. Retrospective accounts can leave important details unmeasured.

visual.caption: Risk describes probability under conditions, not a verdict about one family.

concepts.title: Support changes a developmental pathway.

terms.Protective factor: condition that can reduce adverse risk

points: Protective factor: condition that can reduce adverse risk
Probabilistic: concerning likelihood rather than certainty
Developmental pathway: pattern of change over time
concepts.text:
Protective factor: condition that can reduce adverse risk. Probabilistic: concerning likelihood rather than certainty. Developmental pathway: pattern of change over time.

Healthcare access and supportive environments can influence later opportunities. Biological and social development continue to interact after birth.

Avoid assigning blame from a simplified origin story. Ask what is known now and which practical supports are appropriate, without promising that support reverses every possible effect.

title: Small actions, larger questions
objective: Distinguish infant task performance from an unrestricted claim about what an infant knows.
story: A visitor’s baby looks longer when a toy unexpectedly disappears. Leo says this proves the baby understands every rule about objects. Sam asks what looking time actually tells the researchers.

concepts.title: Infants provide indirect evidence.
points: Habituation: reduced responding with repeated stimulation
Dishabituation: renewed responding after a change
Looking time: duration of visual attention
concepts.text:
Habituation: reduced responding with repeated stimulation. Dishabituation: renewed responding after a change. Looking time: duration of visual attention.

Infants cannot explain an answer verbally. Researchers therefore use responses such as looking, reaching or sucking under defined conditions.

A renewed look can indicate discrimination or novelty. It does not by itself reveal a complete adult-like concept. Visual salience and familiarity are alternative explanations to test.

concepts.title: Different tasks ask different questions.
points: Object permanence: understanding that objects continue unseen
Task demand: what successful performance requires
Converging evidence: support from different suitable methods
concepts.text:
Object permanence: understanding that objects continue unseen. Task demand: what successful performance requires.

Searching for a hidden object requires remembering a location and coordinating action. A looking task has different demands.

Different ages of success across tasks need not mean one method is useless. Compare the specific ability each task requires and seek converging evidence before making a broad claim.

concepts.title: Early learning is active and situated.

terms.Contingent response: response related to a preceding signal

points: Joint attention: sharing attention toward something
Contingent response: response related to a preceding signal
Individual variation: differences among developmental paths
concepts.text:
Joint attention: sharing attention toward something. Contingent response: response related to a preceding signal. Individual variation: differences among developmental paths.

Infants learn through perception, movement and interaction with caregivers. Shared attention can support learning about objects and words.

Developmental milestones describe useful patterns of change, with variation. A casual observation is not a developmental assessment. Persistent concerns are a reason to seek appropriate professional advice.

visual.caption: Use developmental findings without assessing a child from a single episode.

evidence:
Infant methods provide valuable evidence when comparison events control low-level differences and results replicate. Different measures can produce different developmental estimates.

The fictional toy event does not demonstrate a universal timetable, intelligence score or diagnosis.

title: Learning with a little help
objective: Design support that distinguishes independent performance from performance with assistance.
story: Jo helps a younger visitor sort donated buttons. The visitor succeeds after Jo points to one example, then struggles when the rule changes. Leo calls the first success proof of independent mastery.

concepts.title: Thinking changes through activity.

terms.Assimilation: interpreting experience using an existing schema
terms.Accommodation: changing a schema to fit experience

points: Schema: organized understanding of a situation
Assimilation: interpreting experience using an existing schema
Accommodation: changing a schema to fit experience
concepts.text:
Schema: organized understanding of a situation. Assimilation: interpreting experience using an existing schema. Accommodation: changing a schema to fit experience.

Piaget described children as actively constructing understanding. New experiences can fit an existing way of thinking or require revising it.

His broad stages remain historically influential, but performance also varies with task wording, experience and support. Do not use a stage label as a complete account of a particular child.

terms.Scaffolding: temporary support adjusted to a task

points: Zone of proximal development: gap between independent and supported performance
Scaffolding: temporary support adjusted to a task
Guided participation: learning through supported shared activity
concepts.text:
Zone of proximal development: gap between independent and supported performance. Scaffolding: temporary support adjusted to a task. Guided participation: learning through supported shared activity.

Vygotsky emphasized learning in social and cultural activity. Success with guidance identifies what is possible with that support.

Jo can model one comparison, invite the visitor to explain, then reduce help. Independent performance needs a later attempt without the prompt and a suitable new example.

title: Security is a relationship question
objective: Explain attachment as a context-sensitive relationship pattern without assigning a fixed identity.
story: A young visitor stays close to a caregiver in the noisy café, then explores once the caregiver joins the table. Leo wants to label the child’s attachment from that brief visit.

concepts.title: Closeness can support exploration.

terms.Attachment: a bond supporting proximity and safety

points: Attachment: a bond supporting proximity and safety
Secure base: a caregiver relationship supporting exploration
Safe haven: comfort sought when distressed
concepts.text:
Secure base: a caregiver relationship supporting exploration. Safe haven: comfort sought when distressed.

Attachment theory concerns how relationships support safety and exploration, particularly under stress. Staying close in an unfamiliar room can have several explanations.

A short café visit cannot classify a child or caregiver. Researchers use structured procedures and consider the relationship and context being measured.

visual.caption: The sequence is illustrative, not an assessment of attachment security.

concepts.title: A pattern is not an identity.

terms.Temperament: early differences in reactivity and regulation
terms.Caregiving sensitivity: noticing and responding appropriately to signals

points: Attachment pattern: observed relationship-related organization
Temperament: early differences in reactivity and regulation
Caregiving sensitivity: noticing and responding appropriately to signals
concepts.text:
Attachment pattern: observed relationship-related organization. Caregiving sensitivity: noticing and responding appropriately to signals.

Temperament and attachment address different questions. A child may react strongly to noise without having an insecure relationship.

Attachment classifications summarize behavior in specified circumstances. They are not moral ratings, permanent personality types or diagnoses from a single behavior.

visual.caption: The constructs overlap in influences but are not interchangeable.

concepts.title: Relationships develop in wider conditions.
points: Responsiveness: appropriate response to another’s signals
Continuity: persistence across time
Change: variation in later relationship experience
concepts.text:
Responsiveness: appropriate response to another’s signals. Continuity: persistence across time. Change: variation in later relationship experience.

Responsive care matters, but caregiving occurs within work, health, housing and cultural conditions. Children can form attachments with more than one caregiver.

Early patterns can be associated with later outcomes without determining them. Later relationships and changing circumstances also contribute to development.

visual.caption: Developmental associations do not determine one person’s future.

evidence:
Attachment evidence uses relationship-specific measures and longitudinal comparisons. Cultural practices, measurement and stress conditions affect interpretation.

Early associations with later outcomes are probabilistic. They do not show that one behavior identifies a permanent attachment style or parental fault.

Ecological approach: development within interacting contexts

title: Adolescence is more than a warning label
objective: Explain adolescent decisions using context and development without treating age as incapacity.
hook: Adolescence is more than a warning label
story: Jo checks a repair carefully when working alone but rushes during a lively public demonstration. Leo says teenagers cannot make sound decisions. Maya points to Jo’s careful work earlier that day.

concepts.title: Development is uneven and contextual.

terms.Adolescence: transition involving biological and social changes

points: Puberty: biological changes toward sexual maturation
Adolescence: transition involving biological and social changes
Self-regulation: regulating attention, emotion and action
concepts.text:
Self-regulation: regulating attention, emotion and action.

Puberty and adolescence are related but not identical. Physical development, opportunities and social expectations can change on different schedules.

Adolescents often show sophisticated reasoning. Decision quality varies with experience, arousal, incentives and social context. Average developmental patterns do not determine an individual’s competence.

Offer real choices within clear safety boundaries. A supervised practice opportunity can teach a skill more directly than an age stereotype or a vague demand to be sensible.

points: Group average: summary across a sample

title: Adult lives take different routes
objective: Distinguish a socially patterned transition from a universal developmental requirement.
story: Sam returns to study while Pat starts volunteering after leaving paid work. Leo describes both as behind schedule. Maya asks whose timetable he is using.

concepts.title: A life path is not one universal sequence.

terms.Life course: a trajectory embedded in history and society

points: Social clock: cultural expectations about timing
Life transition: change in roles or circumstances
Life course: a trajectory embedded in history and society
concepts.text:
Social clock: cultural expectations about timing. Life transition: change in roles or circumstances. Life course: a trajectory embedded in history and society.

Education, work, partnership and caring roles occur in different orders and at different times. Norms about timing depend on social conditions and culture.

A transition can offer opportunities and strain. Being unusual relative to a local expectation is not evidence of developmental failure.

visual.title: Timing needs a reference
visual.caption: A cultural timetable does not define universal psychological success.

concepts.title: Roles interact with resources.

terms.Role strain: difficulty meeting demands of a role

points: Role strain: difficulty meeting demands of a role
Linked lives: interdependence of life trajectories
Selection: choosing goals or activities
concepts.text:
Role strain: difficulty meeting demands of a role. Linked lives: interdependence of life trajectories. Selection: choosing goals or activities.

A return to study depends on money, care responsibilities, health and opportunity as well as motivation. Changes in one person’s work can affect the whole household.

Ask which demands changed and which resources are available. An individual preference does not explain every constraint or outcome.

visual.title: Understand a transition
visual.caption: A transition is understood through demands, resources and relationships.

concepts.title: Adaptation can change the goal or the route.

terms.Optimization: investing resources in a selected goal
terms.Compensation: using another method when a route is limited

points: Optimization: investing resources in a selected goal
Compensation: using another method when a route is limited
Agency: capacity to act within circumstances
concepts.text:
Optimization: investing resources in a selected goal. Compensation: using another method when a route is limited. Agency: capacity to act within circumstances.

Lifespan accounts distinguish selecting goals, optimizing resources and compensating for constraints. Pat may choose fewer projects, practise a new skill and use an accessible tool.

These are descriptive strategies, not a promise that individuals can overcome every structural barrier. Support and access remain part of the explanation.

visual.title: Several routes to adaptation
visual.caption: Adaptation can involve changing priorities as well as improving performance.

evidence:
Lifespan models describe varied pathways rather than prescribe a single life timetable. Much adult-development evidence is observational and shaped by historical opportunity.

An adaptation framework does not establish that every constraint can be overcome through effort or attitude.
